points.title: Hypotheses and investigable questions
points.brief: An investigable question can be answered by collecting data. A hypothesis is a testable explanation that predicts what will happen if it is right.

points.title: Validity, reliability and accuracy
points.brief: A valid test measures what it aims to and controls other variables, reliable results come out the same when repeated, and accurate results are close to the true value.

points.title: Science and pseudoscience
points.brief: Science tests claims with evidence and changes its mind when the evidence does. Pseudoscience looks scientific but avoids testing, relies on stories and never changes.

points.title: Judging claims and sources
points.brief: Check who made a claim and why, whether the evidence and sample are good enough, and whether a graph's scale or selected data could mislead.

points.title: Large datasets and descriptive statistics
points.brief: Large datasets, such as weather or health records, are summed up with the mean, median, mode and range, and with graphs, to show patterns clearly.

points.title: Correlation and causation
points.brief: Two variables that change together are correlated, but that does not prove one causes the other. A third factor or chance may explain the link.

points.title: Energy efficiency
points.brief: In any device the total energy out equals the energy in, but some is wasted, often as heat. Efficiency is the useful energy out divided by the energy in, as a percentage.

points.title: Generating electricity
points.brief: Electricity is made from non-renewable sources, such as coal and gas, and renewable ones, such as solar, wind and hydro, each with costs and benefits for cost, emissions and reliability.

points.title: Future energy demand
points.brief: Energy use has grown with population and technology. Trends in the data help predict future demand and explain why cleaner energy sources are being developed.

points.title: Circuits and circuit diagrams
points.brief: A complete circuit needs a power source, a closed path of wires and a load, and circuit diagrams draw each part with a standard symbol.

points.title: Series and parallel circuits
points.brief: In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere and passes through each part in turn. In a parallel circuit the current splits between branches.

points.title: Ohm's law
points.brief: Voltage equals current times resistance (V = IR), so for a fixed resistance the current rises as the voltage rises.

points.title: Electrical energy and star ratings
points.brief: An appliance uses more energy the higher its power and the longer it runs, and energy star ratings compare how efficiently similar appliances use it.

points.title: Mechanical and electromagnetic waves
points.brief: Waves carry energy without carrying matter along. Mechanical waves, such as sound, need a medium, while electromagnetic waves, such as light, can travel through a vacuum.

points.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
points.brief: In a transverse wave particles move at right angles to the wave's direction. In a longitudinal wave, such as sound, they move back and forth along it.

points.title: The wave equation
points.brief: Waves are described by wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed, and wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.

points.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
points.brief: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays differ in wavelength and energy, which decides their uses and risks.

points.title: Pitch and loudness
points.brief: Sound travels as compressions and rarefactions. A higher frequency gives a higher pitch, and a larger amplitude gives a louder sound.

points.title: The Doppler effect and ultrasound
points.brief: A sound's pitch rises as its source comes towards us and falls as it moves away. Ultrasound, too high to hear, is reflected inside the body to make medical images.

points.title: Reflection, refraction and absorption
points.brief: Light bounces off surfaces (reflection), bends when it passes into a new material (refraction) and is taken in by dark surfaces (absorption).

points.title: Studying stars with light
points.brief: Splitting a star's light into a spectrum shows which elements it contains and whether it is moving towards or away from us.

points.title: Speed, velocity and displacement
points.brief: Distance is how far something travels and displacement is how far it ends up from the start in a direction. Average velocity is the change in displacement divided by time.

points.title: Acceleration
points.brief: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken, in metres per second squared, and on a velocity-time graph it is the slope.

points.title: Newton's first law
points.brief: An object stays still or keeps moving at a steady velocity unless an unbalanced force, the net force, acts on it. This is inertia.

points.title: Newton's second law
points.brief: Net force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma), so a bigger force or a smaller mass gives a bigger acceleration.

points.title: Newton's third law
points.brief: When one object pushes on another, the second pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction, as when a rocket pushes gas out and the gas pushes it forward.

points.title: Homeostasis
points.brief: The body keeps conditions such as temperature and blood glucose stable, using feedback that reverses any change.

points.title: The nervous system
points.brief: Receptors detect a stimulus, nerves carry fast electrical messages to the brain or spinal cord, and effectors such as muscles respond. A reflex skips the brain.

points.title: The endocrine system
points.brief: Glands release hormones into the blood, which act more slowly and for longer than nerves, such as insulin lowering blood glucose.

points.title: Infectious and non-infectious diseases
points.brief: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread. Non-infectious diseases, such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes, come from genes, lifestyle or environment, and healthy habits lower the risk.

points.title: How pathogens spread
points.brief: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites spread through contact, air, water, food and animals, and hygiene, clean water and isolation slow the spread.

points.title: The body's defences
points.brief: Skin, mucus and stomach acid stop most pathogens getting in. If they do, white blood cells attack them and make antibodies that recognise them next time.

points.title: Vaccination and immunity
points.brief: A vaccine trains the immune system with a harmless form of a pathogen, and when most people are vaccinated, data show the disease becomes rare and protects those who cannot be.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander plant medicines
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have long used plants to prevent and treat illness, such as tea tree leaves used by Bundjalung people on wounds and for coughs.

points.title: DNA, genes and chromosomes
points.brief: DNA carries genetic information. A gene is a section of DNA coding for a trait, and DNA is coiled into chromosomes in the nucleus.

points.title: The double helix
points.brief: DNA is two strands twisted into a double helix, with bases that pair A with T and C with G. Its structure was found using the work of Franklin, Wilkins, Watson and Crick.

points.title: Sexual and asexual reproduction
points.brief: Asexual reproduction makes offspring identical to one parent. Sexual reproduction mixes genes from two parents, so offspring vary.

points.title: Mutations
points.brief: A mutation is a change in DNA. It may be harmful, helpful or have little effect, and only mutations in sex cells pass to offspring.

points.title: Dominant and recessive alleles
points.brief: Each trait has two alleles, one from each parent. A dominant allele shows over a recessive one, and a Punnett square predicts the chances of each genotype and phenotype in offspring.

points.title: Genetic technologies and testing
points.brief: Genetic engineering, cloning and genetic testing are used in medicine, farming, industry and conservation, and raise social, economic and ethical questions such as privacy.

points.title: Natural selection
points.brief: Individuals vary, and those with traits better suited to the environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations.

points.title: Evidence for evolution
points.brief: Fossils, similar bone structures in different animals and shared DNA show that species have changed over time and share common ancestors.

points.title: Darwin, Wallace and the theory of evolution
points.brief: Darwin and Wallace each proposed natural selection from their observations, and later evidence from genetics strengthened and refined the theory.

points.title: Aboriginal rock art as a record of change
points.brief: Some Aboriginal rock art shows animals no longer found in that area, such as the thylacine in Arnhem Land, recording changes in plants and animals over thousands of years.

points.title: Weather and climate
points.brief: Weather is the conditions over hours or days. Climate is the average pattern over 30 years or more, shaped by natural processes such as ocean currents and volcanic eruptions.

points.title: The enhanced greenhouse effect
points.brief: Greenhouse gases trap heat that keeps Earth warm. Burning fossil fuels since industrialisation has added more of them, strengthening the natural effect into the enhanced greenhouse effect, so global temperatures have risen.

points.title: Impacts of climate change
points.brief: Satellites and other data show rising sea levels, warmer oceans and shrinking ice, and climate change alters the water cycle and puts ecosystems under stress.

points.title: Reducing emissions
points.brief: Emissions can be cut by renewable energy, using less energy and capturing carbon, and each method has advantages and limits.

points.title: Pollution
points.brief: Human activities pollute air, water and soil, such as plastics in oceans and fertiliser running into rivers, harming living things and people's health.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander sustainable harvesting
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples developed harvesting practices from deep ecological knowledge, such as taking only part of a resource and following seasons, so it lasts.

points.title: Reduce, reuse and recycle
points.brief: Using less, reusing items and recycling materials such as aluminium, paper and plastic saves resources and energy, and scientists keep finding new ways to recycle.

points.title: Ions and ionic bonding
points.brief: Atoms gain or lose electrons to get a full outer shell, forming ions. Metal and non-metal ions attract in ionic compounds, such as sodium chloride (NaCl).

points.title: Covalent bonding
points.brief: Non-metal atoms share electrons to form molecules, such as water, and some elements, such as oxygen (O2), exist as pairs of atoms.

points.title: Metallic bonding
points.brief: In metals, positive ions sit in a sea of shared electrons that can move, which is why metals conduct electricity and can be bent.

points.title: Properties from bonding
points.brief: Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct when dissolved, covalent molecules often have low melting points, and these properties decide their uses.

points.title: Organic compounds and hydrocarbons
points.brief: Organic compounds are based on carbon, and hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Most come from crude oil, natural gas and living things.

points.title: Fractional distillation of crude oil
points.brief: Crude oil is heated and its parts separate in a tall column by boiling point, giving products such as petrol, diesel and bitumen.

points.title: Naming alkanes
points.brief: Alkanes with one to eight carbons are named methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane, hexane, heptane and octane, and drawn with their bonds.

points.title: Complete and incomplete combustion
points.brief: With enough oxygen, hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water. With too little, they also make carbon monoxide and soot and release less energy.

points.title: Australia's mineral resources
points.brief: Australia mines minerals such as iron ore, bauxite and coal, which are finite, and extracting them can damage land, water and habitats.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander uses of minerals
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have used minerals for many purposes, such as ochre for paint and ceremony and hard stone for axes and grinding tools.

points.title: Polymers and plastics
points.brief: Polymers are long chains of small repeating molecules, mostly made from crude oil. Many plastics last for centuries in the environment, so alternatives are being developed.

points.title: Conservation of mass
points.brief: In a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged, not made or destroyed, so in a closed system the total mass stays the same.

points.title: Balanced chemical equations
points.brief: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides, with states shown as (s), (l), (g) and (aq).

points.title: Types of reactions
points.brief: Common reactions include combustion, decomposition, precipitation, where two solutions form an insoluble solid, and acids reacting with metals or carbonates.

points.title: Acids, bases and neutralisation
points.brief: The pH scale runs from acidic below 7 to basic above 7, with pure water at 7. An acid and a base neutralise each other to make a salt and water.

points.title: Rates of reaction
points.brief: Reactions go faster at higher temperature, higher concentration, with more surface area or with a catalyst, because particles collide more often or with more energy.

points.title: Where elements come from
points.brief: Hydrogen and helium formed soon after the Big Bang, and heavier elements formed later by fusion inside stars.

points.title: Radioactive decay and half-life
points.brief: An unstable nucleus gives off alpha, beta or gamma radiation as it decays. Half-life is the time for half the atoms in a sample to decay.

points.title: Uses of radioisotopes
points.brief: Radioisotopes are used to find and treat cancer, sterilise equipment, check for leaks and date ancient materials, with care because radiation can harm cells.

points.title: Fission and fusion
points.brief: Fission splits a heavy nucleus, as in nuclear power stations, which leave radioactive waste. Fusion joins light nuclei, as in the Sun. Both release huge amounts of energy.
